web.tagline: Read, encode, compare and edit DNA sequences.

learn.title: What DNA is
learn.about: DNA is the molecule that stores the instructions to build and run every living thing, from a bacterium to a person. It's in almost all of your cells, and it's written with just four letters.

complement.title: Double helix
complement.about: Type one DNA strand and see its partner. The two strands run in opposite directions, so the complement is written backwards to read it from 5' to 3'.

transcribe.title: Transcription
transcribe.about: Copies the DNA coding strand into messenger RNA: every T becomes U.

translate.title: Translation
translate.about: Reads RNA like a ribosome: it starts at the first AUG, moves 3 bases at a time and stops at the first stop codon.

protein.title: 3D protein
protein.about: Type a gene: its reading frame is found, the protein is identified in UniProt (BLAST) and its AlphaFold DB structure is shown. If yours is different or invented, it is predicted with ESMFold and compared with the natural one. Then you can explore it in the 3D microscope.

to_binary.title: DNA to binary
to_binary.about: Each base takes 2 bits: A = 00, C = 01, G = 10 and T = 11. Each base and its partner are bitwise opposites.

from_binary.title: Binary to DNA
from_binary.about: Reads the bits 2 at a time and turns them into bases. You can separate the bits with spaces.

being.title: Being from bits
being.about: Generates random bits and reads them as DNA. Operations add up: flipping the bits twice brings back the original being.

find.title: Find
find.about: Finds where a fragment appears inside a sequence.

align.title: Align
align.about: Places one sequence under the other, with gaps where needed, so they match as closely as possible (Needleman-Wunsch algorithm).

permutations.title: Permutations
permutations.about: Every distinct sequence you can make by reordering the bases, with no repeats.

crispr.title: CRISPR/Cas9
crispr.about: Find where Cas9 can cut, pick a target and decide how the cell repairs the cut.

microscope.title: 3D microscope
microscope.about: Fly inside your sequence: from the double helix to an atom, its nucleus, a proton and its quarks. With keyboard, mouse or touch screen.

learn.lead: DNA is the molecule that stores the instructions to build and run every living thing, from a bacterium to a person. It's in almost all of your cells, and it's written with just four letters.

letters.title: Four chemical letters
letters.p1: DNA is a very long chain of pieces called nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugars and phosphates link together to form the backbone of the chain; the bases stick out from it and carry the information.
letters.p2: DNA has four bases, which is why it's written with four letters: A, G, C and T. By their shape, they fall into two families.
letters.T: Pairs with adenine. It's only found in DNA, and it's like uracil with one extra methyl group (CH₃).
letters.U: Takes the place of thymine in RNA.
letters.key: How to read the pictures: the balls are hydrogen (H), nitrogen (N) and oxygen (O) atoms, and the unlabeled corners of the rings are carbon atoms. Double lines are double bonds.

pairs.title: Pairs that fit
pairs.p1: The bases on one strand bind to those on the other through hydrogen bonds: weak attractions that can open and close without breaking the chain. Only two pairs fit.
pairs.p2: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so every rung is the same length and the double helix keeps a constant width of about 2 nanometers. And since each base accepts only one partner, knowing one strand is enough to know the other.

helix.title: The double helix
helix.p1: The two strands wind around each other like a spiral staircase: the steps are the base pairs, and the handrails are the sugar-phosphate backbones. The staircase makes a full turn every 10.5 base pairs, about 3.5 nanometers.
helix.p2: The strands run in opposite directions. Each has one end called 5' and another called 3', after the sugar carbon where it ends, and they're laid out back to front relative to each other: they're antiparallel.
helix.p3: This shape was described by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, based on X-ray images taken by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, especially the famous Photo 51.

copy.title: How it's copied
copy.p1: Before it divides, a cell has to copy all of its DNA. The enzyme helicase separates the two strands like opening a zipper, and DNA polymerase builds a new strand opposite each one, following the pairing rules.
copy.p2: In the end there are two identical molecules, and each keeps one strand from the original: that's why copying is called semiconservative. Polymerase rarely makes mistakes, and it also checks its work and fixes almost all of them.

protein.title: From DNA to proteins
protein.p1: In cells like ours, DNA never leaves the nucleus. To use a gene, the cell first makes a working copy in messenger RNA: that's transcription. RNA is written almost like DNA, but it uses uracil (U) instead of thymine.
protein.p2: Next, the ribosome reads that RNA three bases at a time. Each group of three, called a codon, stands for one amino acid. There are 64 possible codons for only 20 amino acids, so several codons mean the same thing. Reading starts at the AUG codon and ends at one of three stop codons: UAA, UAG or UGA. That's translation.
protein.p3: The chain of amino acids folds up into a protein, like the enzymes that digest food, the hemoglobin that carries oxygen or the keratin in hair.

mutations.title: When DNA changes
mutations.p1: Sometimes one base is swapped for another, or a few are lost or added: these are mutations. Many have no effect at all, some cause disease and a few turn out to be useful. They're the raw material of evolution.
mutations.p2: Because the ribosome reads three bases at a time, adding or removing a single base shifts all the reading after it and changes every following amino acid. If the change is three bases long, the reading falls back into step.
mutations.p3: Today DNA can be edited on purpose with CRISPR/Cas9, a tool that cuts DNA at the exact spot a guide RNA points to. Its development earned Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

info.title: DNA as information
info.p1: With four letters, each base can store 2 bits: A = 00, C = 01, G = 10 and T = 11. Your genome has about 3.1 billion base pairs per set of chromosomes; written that way, it would take up about 775 megabytes.
info.p2: If you stretched out the DNA from just one of your cells, it would be about 2 meters long. It fits in a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimeter across because it's wound around proteins and folded over itself many times.
info.p3: It's so dense that books, images and videos have already been stored in DNA made in the lab.

helix.title: DNA · {sequence}
explanation: Two strands wound into a spiral; each turn is 3.55 nm long
and has 10.5 base pairs (B form, the one found in cells).
explanation_base: Each base is joined to its partner by hydrogen bonds
(yellow lines): A–T makes 2 and G–C makes 3.
explanation_sugar: Deoxyribose links the base to the phosphate.
Sugars and phosphates make the «handrails» of the ladder.
explanation_phosphate: The phosphate is negatively charged: that is why DNA is an acid.
It links the sugar of one nucleotide to the next.
helix.time: 1 s on screen ≈ 50 fs in reality (bond vibrations slowed down ~10¹³ times)
explanation_atomic: Atomic mode: every atom drawn as in AtomicWorld, with all its shells.
Colours by shell: orange n = 1, cyan n = 2, violet n = 3 (phosphorus).
explanation_plastic: Plastic mode: go into an atom (Enter) to see its electrons (e⁻),
and in its nucleus, the protons (+), neutrons (0) and quarks (u, d).

nucleus_explanation: Radius ≈ {r} fm: the atom is ~{ratio} times bigger.
Almost all of the atom's mass is here. Get closer (or press Enter) to go in.
cloud_explanation: Each dot is a likely position of an electron, not a path: they do not orbit.
Colours: orange n = 1, cyan n = 2, violet n = 3; p orbitals show their lobes.
Where the clouds overlap with their neighbours, electrons are shared: that is the bond.
cloud_explanation_realistic: Isolated atom: averaged over all orientations, its density is spherical.
In the molecule the orbitals deform when they bond (not shown here).
atom.time: Stationary orbitals: the density does not change (the flicker = successive measurements)

cloud_explanation: Each dot is a likely position of an electron: this is how AtomicWorld draws the atom.
Colours by shell: orange n = 1, cyan n = 2, violet n = 3. Inner shells are fainter.
Neighbour clouds are fainter. O: one subshell at a time · I: one p orbital.

shape.s: s orbital: a sphere (with {nodes} spherical nodes inside).
shape.p: p orbitals: two lobes (a figure of eight) along x, y or z.
shape.d: d orbitals: four-leaf clovers, and dz²: two lobes with a ring around the middle.
shape.f: f orbitals: six or eight lobes; the most complex shapes in the ground states.

atomic.hund: Hund's rule: electrons first take empty orbitals (↑), then pair up (↑↓).
atomic.full: Full subshell: its orbitals add up to a perfect sphere (Unsöld's theorem).
atomic.partial: Partly filled: several states are equally good; this is one of them.
atomic.orbital_colors: Each orbital in its own colour. I: one orbital at a time.

explanation: Plastic mode: each green ball (e⁻) is an electron. They orbit as in Bohr's model (1913).
In reality they have no size and no path: they are probability clouds (Tab: other modes).
In the centre, the nucleus with its protons (+) and neutrons (0), to scale: tiny.

nucleus.title: {protons} + {neutrons} · radius ≈ {r} fm
explanation: The strong force beats the electric repulsion between the {protons}.
Probability of finding an electron in here: ~{p_in}
A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh ~1 billion tonnes.
explanation_hydrogen: The hydrogen-1 nucleus is a single proton.
Probability of finding the electron in here: ~{p_in}
explanation_realistic: Nuclear matter density (Woods–Saxon profile): nucleons are
quantum waves and have no definite position.
nucleus.strong_lines: Green lines: strong nuclear force (range ~2 fm).
nucleus.go_in: get closer (or press Enter) to go in

proton.title: Proton
proton.detail: charge +1 · {mass} MeV/c² · quarks u u d
explanation: 3 valence quarks (uud) held together by gluons.
Only ~1 % of its mass comes from the quarks: the rest is energy
of the strong interaction (E = mc²).

neutron.title: Neutron
neutron.detail: charge 0 · {mass} MeV/c² · quarks u d d
explanation: 3 valence quarks (udd). Free, it decays in ~15 minutes;
inside a stable nucleus it lasts forever.
Without neutrons, electric repulsion would push the protons apart.

nucleus.time: 1 s on screen ≈ 10⁻²² s in reality (a nucleon crosses the nucleus in ~10⁻²² s)
plastic: Plastic mode: protons (+, red) and neutrons (0, blue). The colours are made up.
They are not hard balls: each one is a cloud of quarks and gluons ~0.84 fm in radius.

nucleon.title: {name}: valence quarks {content} + parton sea
nucleon.realistic_detail: 1 s on screen ≈ 10⁻²⁴ s in reality
quark_explanation: Fundamental particle: no known structure (< 10⁻¹⁸ m).
The journey ends here: there is nothing «inside» a quark.
Confinement: if you pull a quark away, the gluon tube
snaps and creates new quark–antiquark pairs.
explanation: Red/green/blue = colour charge (a label, not a real colour).
The 3 quarks add up to «white». Travelling gluons swap
colour between them. Background dots: gluons and sea pairs.
Quarks provide ~1 % of the mass; the rest is energy (E = mc²).
explanation_realistic: Parton fog: quarks, antiquarks and gluons that appear and
disappear. You cannot point to where each quark is: only the
probability of finding them (charge radius 0.84 fm).
nucleon.time: 1 s on screen ≈ 10⁻²⁴ s in reality (light crosses a proton in ~3×10⁻²⁴ s)
plastic: Plastic mode: up (u) and down (d) quarks; the gluon (g) travels from one to another.
The halo of each quark is its colour charge (red, green or blue): a label, not a colour.
Quarks are point-like: here they are balls so you can see them.

protein.title: Protein · {name}
explanation: A chain of amino acids folded onto itself. The coloured line joins the
alpha carbons: yellow hydrophobic, green polar, blue +, red −, grey Gly/Pro.
explanation_confidence: Prediction confidence colours (pLDDT): dark blue very high,
light blue confident, yellow low, orange very low.
explanation_backbone: Backbone: N–Cα–C=O, the same in every amino acid.
The peptide bond (C–N) joins each one to the next.
explanation_sidechain: Side chain: what makes each amino acid different
and decides where it ends up when the protein folds.

classes.hydrophobic: Hydrophobic: avoids water and usually ends up inside the protein.
classes.special: Glycine or proline: the most flexible or the most rigid amino acid in the chain.
classes.polar: Polar: uncharged but attracts water; usually on the surface.
